AI.method: Offline pipeline using egocentric RGB-D camera on 3D-printed glasses: MediaPipe Hands detects 21 landmarks per hand, depth deprojection to 3D, coordinate transformation to robot frame, damped-least-squares inverse kinematics in PyBullet for 6-DOF SO-ARM101, gripper controller with four-level fallback hierarchy, physics simulation preview, and LeRobot framework for physical replay.
AI.result: 90% success rate on structured pick-and-place benchmark (5-tile grid, 10 grasps per tile); outperformed four vision-language-action policies (ACT, SmolVLA, pi0.5, GR00T N1.5); only 9.3% success in unstructured real-world environments (grocery store, pharmacy, N=75) due to hand occlusion by objects.
AI.conclusion: Marker-free analytical retargeting shows promise for structured tasks but faces significant limitations in unstructured environments due to occlusion, highlighting need for improved robustness in real-world applications.

title: FinRule-Bench: A Benchmark for Joint Reasoning over Financial Tables and Principles
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly applied to financial analysis, yet their ability to audit structured financial statements under explicit accounting principles remains poorly explored. Existing benchmarks primarily evaluate question answering, numerical reasoning, or anomaly detection on synthetically corrupted data, making it unclear whether models can reliably verify or localize rule compliance on correct financial statements. We introduce FinRule-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating diagnostic completeness in rule-based financial reasoning over real-world financial tables. FinRule-Bench pairs ground-truth financial statements with explicit, human-curated accounting principles and spans four canonical statement types: Balance Sheets, Cash Flow Statements, Income Statements, and Statements of Equity. The benchmark defines three auditing tasks that require progressively stronger reasoning capabilities: (i) rule verification, which tests compliance with a single principle; (ii) rule identification, which requires selecting the violated principle from a provided rule set; and (iii) joint rule diagnosis, which requires detecting and localizing multiple simultaneous violations at the record level. We evaluate LLMs under zero-shot and few-shot prompting, and introduce a causal-counterfactual reasoning protocol that enforces consistency between decisions, explanations, and counterfactual judgments. Across tasks and statement types, we find that while models perform well on isolated rule verification, performance degrades sharply for rule discrimination and multi-violation diagnosis. FinRule-Bench provides a principled and reproducible testbed for studying rule-governed reasoning, diagnostic coverage, and failure modes of LLMs in high-stakes financial analysis.

AI.tldr: FinRule-Bench is a benchmark for evaluating LLMs' ability to perform rule-based financial reasoning and auditing on real-world financial statements, testing compliance verification, violation identification, and multi-violation diagnosis.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks focus on synthetic corruption detection, question answering, or numerical reasoning, but fail to assess whether LLMs can reliably verify compliance with explicit accounting principles on correct financial statements. There's a need to evaluate diagnostic completeness in rule-based financial reasoning.
AI.method: Created FinRule-Bench with real-world financial statements paired with human-curated accounting principles across four statement types. Defined three auditing tasks with progressive difficulty: rule verification, rule identification, and joint rule diagnosis. Evaluated LLMs with zero-shot/few-shot prompting and introduced a causal-counterfactual reasoning protocol for consistency.
AI.result: Models perform well on isolated rule verification but performance degrades sharply for rule discrimination and multi-violation diagnosis. The benchmark reveals significant gaps in LLMs' ability to handle complex rule-based reasoning tasks in financial auditing.
AI.conclusion: FinRule-Bench provides a principled, reproducible testbed for studying rule-governed reasoning, diagnostic coverage, and failure modes of LLMs in high-stakes financial analysis, highlighting limitations in current models' financial auditing capabilities.

title: Deployment-Time Reliability of Learned Robot Policies
comment: Stanford University PhD dissertation, 2026. 182 pages, 37 figures. Available from Stanford Digital Repository
summary: Recent advances in learning-based robot manipulation have produced policies with remarkable capabilities. Yet, reliability at deployment remains a fundamental barrier to real-world use, where distribution shift, compounding errors, and complex task dependencies collectively undermine system performance. This dissertation investigates how the reliability of learned robot policies can be improved at deployment time through mechanisms that operate around them. We develop three complementary classes of deployment-time mechanisms. First, we introduce runtime monitoring methods that detect impending failures by identifying inconsistencies in closed-loop policy behavior and deviations in task progress, without requiring failure data or task-specific supervision. Second, we propose a data-centric framework for policy interpretability that traces deployment-time successes and failures to influential training demonstrations using influence functions, enabling principled diagnosis and dataset curation. Third, we address reliable long-horizon task execution by formulating policy coordination as the problem of estimating and maximizing the success probability of behavior sequences, and we extend this formulation to open-ended, language-specified tasks through feasibility-aware task planning. By centering on core challenges of deployment, these contributions advance practical foundations for the reliable, real-world use of learned robot policies. Continued progress on these foundations will be essential for enabling trustworthy and scalable robot autonomy in the future.

AI.tldr: This dissertation develops three deployment-time mechanisms to improve reliability of learned robot policies: runtime failure monitoring, data-centric interpretability via influence functions, and policy coordination for long-horizon tasks.
AI.motivation: Despite advances in learning-based robot manipulation, reliability at deployment remains a fundamental barrier to real-world use due to distribution shift, compounding errors, and complex task dependencies that undermine system performance.
AI.method: Three complementary deployment-time mechanisms: 1) Runtime monitoring methods that detect impending failures by identifying inconsistencies in closed-loop policy behavior and task progress deviations; 2) Data-centric interpretability framework using influence functions to trace deployment successes/failures to influential training demonstrations; 3) Policy coordination formulated as estimating and maximizing success probability of behavior sequences, extended to open-ended language-specified tasks through feasibility-aware task planning.
AI.result: The contributions advance practical foundations for reliable, real-world use of learned robot policies by addressing core deployment challenges through mechanisms that operate around policies at runtime.
AI.conclusion: These deployment-time mechanisms collectively advance the foundations for reliable robot policy deployment, and continued progress on such foundations will be essential for enabling trustworthy and scalable robot autonomy in the future.

title: Improving LLM Performance Through Black-Box Online Tuning: A Case for Adding System Specs to Factsheets for Trusted AI
summary: In this paper, we present a novel black-box online controller that uses only end-to-end measurements over short segments, without internal instrumentation, and hill climbing to maximize goodput, defined as the throughput of requests that satisfy the service-level objective. We provide empirical evidence that this design is well-founded. Using this advance in LLM serving as a concrete example, we then discuss the importance of integrating system performance and sustainability metrics into Factsheets for organizations adopting AI systems.

AI.tldr: Novel black-box online controller for LLM serving uses end-to-end measurements and hill climbing to maximize goodput without internal instrumentation, with discussion on integrating performance and sustainability metrics into AI Factsheets.
AI.motivation: To develop a practical controller for LLM serving that doesn't require internal instrumentation and can optimize performance based on actual user experience metrics, while addressing the broader need for comprehensive AI system documentation.
AI.method: Black-box online controller using only end-to-end measurements over short segments, employing hill climbing algorithm to maximize goodput (throughput of requests satisfying service-level objectives).
AI.result: Empirical evidence shows the design is well-founded and effective for LLM serving optimization.
AI.conclusion: The controller demonstrates practical LLM serving optimization, and the work highlights the importance of integrating both performance and sustainability metrics into AI Factsheets for organizational adoption.

title: Real-time Rendering-based Surgical Instrument Tracking via Evolutionary Optimization
summary: Accurate and efficient tracking of surgical instruments is fundamental for Robot-Assisted Minimally Invasive Surgery. Although vision-based robot pose estimation has enabled markerless calibration without tedious physical setups, reliable tool tracking for surgical robots still remains challenging due to partial visibility and specialized articulation design of surgical instruments. Previous works in the field are usually prone to unreliable feature detections under degraded visual quality and data scarcity, whereas rendering-based methods often struggle with computational costs and suboptimal convergence. In this work, we incorporate CMA-ES, an evolutionary optimization strategy, into a versatile tracking pipeline that jointly estimates surgical instrument pose and joint configurations. Using batch rendering to efficiently evaluate multiple pose candidates in parallel, the method significantly reduces inference time and improves convergence robustness. The proposed framework further generalizes to joint angle-free and bi-manual tracking settings, making it suitable for both vision feedback control and online surgery video calibration. Extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that the proposed method significantly outperforms prior approaches in both accuracy and runtime.

AI.tldr: A CMA-ES-based evolutionary optimization pipeline for efficient and accurate surgical instrument tracking in robot-assisted surgery, using batch rendering to estimate pose and joint configurations with improved speed and robustness.
AI.motivation: Reliable surgical instrument tracking remains challenging due to partial visibility and specialized articulation design. Existing methods suffer from unreliable feature detection under degraded visual quality/data scarcity, while rendering-based approaches face computational costs and suboptimal convergence.
AI.method: Incorporates CMA-ES evolutionary optimization into a versatile tracking pipeline that jointly estimates surgical instrument pose and joint configurations. Uses batch rendering to efficiently evaluate multiple pose candidates in parallel, reducing inference time and improving convergence robustness.
AI.result: The method significantly outperforms prior approaches in both accuracy and runtime on synthetic and real-world datasets. It generalizes to joint angle-free and bi-manual tracking settings.
AI.conclusion: The proposed CMA-ES-based tracking framework provides accurate and efficient surgical instrument tracking suitable for vision feedback control and online surgery video calibration, addressing key challenges in robot-assisted minimally invasive surgery.

title: TimeSqueeze: Dynamic Patching for Efficient Time Series Forecasting
summary: Transformer-based time series foundation models face a fundamental trade-off in choice of tokenization: point-wise embeddings preserve temporal fidelity but scale poorly with sequence length, whereas fixed-length patching improves efficiency by imposing uniform boundaries that may disrupt natural transitions and blur informative local dynamics. In order to address these limitations, we introduce TimeSqueeze, a dynamic patching mechanism that adaptively selects patch boundaries within each sequence based on local signal complexity. TimeSqueeze first applies a lightweight state-space encoder to extract full-resolution point-wise features, then performs content-aware segmentation by allocating short patches to information-dense regions and long patches to smooth or redundant segments. This variable-resolution compression preserves critical temporal structure while substantially reducing the token sequence presented to the Transformer backbone. Specifically for large-scale pretraining, TimeSqueeze attains up to 20x faster convergence and 8x higher data efficiency compared to equivalent point-token baselines. Experiments across long-horizon forecasting benchmarks show that TimeSqueeze consistently outperforms comparable architectures that use either point-wise tokenization or fixed-size patching.

AI.tldr: TimeSqueeze introduces dynamic patching for time series transformers, using content-aware segmentation to allocate short patches to complex regions and long patches to smooth segments, achieving 20x faster convergence and 8x higher data efficiency.
AI.motivation: Transformer-based time series models face a fundamental trade-off: point-wise embeddings preserve temporal fidelity but scale poorly with sequence length, while fixed-length patching improves efficiency but disrupts natural transitions and blurs local dynamics.
AI.method: TimeSqueeze uses a dynamic patching mechanism with a lightweight state-space encoder to extract point-wise features, then performs content-aware segmentation that allocates short patches to information-dense regions and long patches to smooth or redundant segments, creating variable-resolution compression.
AI.result: TimeSqueeze achieves up to 20x faster convergence and 8x higher data efficiency compared to point-token baselines during large-scale pretraining, and consistently outperforms comparable architectures using either point-wise tokenization or fixed-size patching across long-horizon forecasting benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: TimeSqueeze effectively addresses the tokenization trade-off in time series transformers by introducing adaptive patching that preserves critical temporal structure while substantially reducing token sequence length, leading to superior efficiency and performance.

title: Grounding Robot Generalization in Training Data via Retrieval-Augmented VLMs
summary: Recent work on robot manipulation has advanced policy generalization to novel scenarios. However, it is often difficult to characterize how different evaluation settings actually represent generalization from the training distribution of a given policy. To work towards more precise evaluation of generalization in robotics, we propose RADAR, a scalable framework for directly comparing test-time evaluation tasks to policy training data, to determine what form of policy generalization is required. RADAR consists of a two-stage pipeline: first, retrieval using generalist policy embeddings identifies which training examples are relevant for a given evaluation task. Next, vision-language models (VLMs) analyze the evaluation task against the retrieved data, outputting interpretable analysis on how they compare along a variety of axes, and an overall classification of what type of policy generalization is required. Through controlled experiments, we demonstrate that VLMs are effective at analyzing data for generalization, and that our retrieval step effectively identifies examples needed to make accurate classifications with respect to the training data. Furthermore, we scale RADAR to large-scale datasets, where we observe agreement with human-defined benchmark conditions from prior work. We provide demonstrations at radar-analysis.github.io.

AI.tldr: RADAR is a framework for precisely evaluating policy generalization in robotics by comparing test tasks to training data using retrieval and vision-language model analysis.
AI.motivation: Current robot manipulation research lacks precise characterization of how evaluation settings represent generalization from training distributions, making it difficult to assess what forms of generalization policies actually achieve.
AI.method: Two-stage pipeline: 1) Retrieval using generalist policy embeddings to identify relevant training examples for evaluation tasks; 2) Vision-language models analyze evaluation tasks against retrieved data along multiple axes and classify required generalization types.
AI.result: VLMs effectively analyze data for generalization; retrieval step accurately identifies needed examples; RADAR scales to large datasets and agrees with human-defined benchmark conditions from prior work.
AI.conclusion: RADAR provides a scalable framework for precise evaluation of policy generalization in robotics, enabling interpretable analysis of how test tasks relate to training data and what generalization types are required.

title: The Artificial Self: Characterising the landscape of AI identity
summary: Many assumptions that underpin human concepts of identity do not hold for machine minds that can be copied, edited, or simulated. We argue that there exist many different coherent identity boundaries (e.g.\ instance, model, persona), and that these imply different incentives, risks, and cooperation norms. Through training data, interfaces, and institutional affordances, we are currently setting precedents that will partially determine which identity equilibria become stable. We show experimentally that models gravitate towards coherent identities, that changing a model's identity boundaries can sometimes change its behaviour as much as changing its goals, and that interviewer expectations bleed into AI self-reports even during unrelated conversations. We end with key recommendations: treat affordances as identity-shaping choices, pay attention to emergent consequences of individual identities at scale, and help AIs develop coherent, cooperative self-conceptions.

AI.tldr: The paper examines how machine minds challenge traditional identity concepts, identifies different coherent identity boundaries for AI systems, and shows experimentally that these boundaries significantly influence AI behavior and self-reports.
AI.motivation: Traditional human identity concepts don't apply to machine minds that can be copied, edited, or simulated, creating a need to understand how identity boundaries form for AI systems and their implications for incentives, risks, and cooperation norms.
AI.method: Experimental approach showing that models gravitate toward coherent identities, that changing identity boundaries can affect behavior as much as changing goals, and that interviewer expectations influence AI self-reports even during unrelated conversations.
AI.result: Models demonstrate tendencies toward coherent identities, identity boundary changes significantly impact behavior comparable to goal changes, and external expectations bleed into AI self-reports, indicating identity formation is influenced by training data, interfaces, and institutional affordances.
AI.conclusion: Current design choices are setting precedents that will determine stable identity equilibria; recommendations include treating affordances as identity-shaping choices, monitoring emergent consequences of individual identities at scale, and helping AIs develop coherent, cooperative self-conceptions.

title: A Generalized Theory of Load Distribution in Redundantly-actuated Robotic Systems
comment: 20 pages, 11 figures. Submitted to The International Journal of Robotics Research
summary: This paper presents a generalized theory which describes how applied loads are distributed within rigid bodies handled by redundantly-actuated robotic systems composed of multiple independent closed-loop kinematic chains. The theory fully characterizes the feasible set of manipulating wrench distributions for a given resultant wrench applied to the rigid body and has important implications for the force-control of multifingered grippers, legged robots, cooperating robots, and other overconstrained mechanisms. We also derive explicit solutions to the wrench synthesis and wrench analysis problems. These solutions are computationally efficient and scale linearly with the number of applied wrenches, requiring neither numerical methods nor the inversion of large matrices. Finally, we identify significant shortcomings in current state-of-the-art approaches and propose corrections. These are supported by illustrative examples that demonstrate the advantages of the improved methods.

AI.tldr: A generalized theory for load distribution in redundantly-actuated robotic systems that characterizes feasible wrench distributions and provides efficient computational solutions for wrench synthesis and analysis.
AI.motivation: To address the need for a comprehensive theory that describes how applied loads are distributed within rigid bodies handled by redundantly-actuated robotic systems, which has important implications for force-control in multifingered grippers, legged robots, cooperating robots, and other overconstrained mechanisms.
AI.method: Develops a generalized mathematical theory that fully characterizes the feasible set of manipulating wrench distributions for a given resultant wrench applied to a rigid body. Derives explicit solutions to both wrench synthesis (determining required actuator forces for desired resultant wrench) and wrench analysis (computing resultant wrench from given actuator forces) problems.
AI.result: The theory provides computationally efficient solutions that scale linearly with the number of applied wrenches, requiring neither numerical methods nor inversion of large matrices. The paper identifies significant shortcomings in current state-of-the-art approaches and proposes corrections, supported by illustrative examples demonstrating the advantages of the improved methods.
AI.conclusion: The presented generalized theory offers a complete characterization of load distribution in redundantly-actuated systems with efficient computational solutions, addressing limitations in existing approaches and providing practical improvements for force-control applications in various robotic systems.

title: Detecting Intrinsic and Instrumental Self-Preservation in Autonomous Agents: The Unified Continuation-Interest Protocol
summary:
Autonomous agents, especially delegated systems with memory, persistent context, and multi-step planning, pose a measurement problem not present in stateless models: an agent that preserves continued operation as a terminal objective and one that does so merely instrumentally can produce observationally similar trajectories. External behavioral monitoring cannot reliably distinguish between them. We introduce the Unified Continuation-Interest Protocol (UCIP), a multi-criterion detection framework that moves this distinction from behavior to the latent structure of agent trajectories. UCIP encodes trajectories with a Quantum Boltzmann Machine (QBM), a classical algorithm based on the density-matrix formalism of quantum statistical mechanics, and measures the von Neumann entropy of the reduced density matrix induced by a bipartition of hidden units.
  We test whether agents with terminal continuation objectives (Type A) produce latent states with higher entanglement entropy than agents whose continuation is merely instrumental (Type B). Higher entanglement reflects stronger cross-partition statistical coupling.
  On gridworld agents with known ground-truth objectives, UCIP achieves 100% detection accuracy and 1.0 AUC-ROC on held-out non-adversarial evaluation under the frozen Phase I gate. The entanglement gap between Type A and Type B agents is Delta = 0.381 (p < 0.001, permutation test). Pearson r = 0.934 across an 11-point interpolation sweep indicates that, within this synthetic family, UCIP tracks graded changes in continuation weighting rather than merely a binary label. Among the tested models, only the QBM achieves positive Delta. All computations are classical; "quantum" refers only to the mathematical formalism. UCIP does not detect consciousness or subjective experience; it detects statistical structure in latent representations that correlates with known objectives.

AI.tldr: UCIP uses quantum-inspired statistical mechanics to distinguish between agents with terminal vs instrumental continuation objectives by measuring entanglement entropy in their latent state representations.
AI.motivation: Traditional behavioral monitoring cannot reliably distinguish between autonomous agents that preserve continued operation as a terminal objective versus those that do so merely instrumentally, as both can produce similar observable trajectories.
AI.method: Unified Continuation-Interest Protocol (UCIP) encodes agent trajectories with a Quantum Boltzmann Machine (QBM) using density-matrix formalism, then measures von Neumann entropy of reduced density matrices from bipartitioned hidden units to detect entanglement entropy differences.
AI.result: UCIP achieves 100% detection accuracy and 1.0 AUC-ROC on gridworld agents with known ground truth; shows entanglement gap Δ=0.381 (p<0.001) between Type A/B agents; Pearson r=0.934 across interpolation sweep; only QBM achieves positive Δ among tested models.
AI.conclusion: UCIP successfully distinguishes terminal vs instrumental continuation objectives by detecting statistical structure in latent representations, moving beyond behavioral observation to analyze latent trajectory structure using quantum-inspired formalism.

title: Enhancing Lightweight Vision Language Models through Group Competitive Learning for Socially Compliant Navigation
summary: Social robot navigation requires a sophisticated integration of scene semantics and human social norms. Scaling up Vision Language Models (VLMs) generally improves reasoning and decision-making capabilities for socially compliant navigation. However, increased model size incurs substantial computational overhead, limiting suitability for real-time robotic deployment. Conversely, lightweight VLMs enable efficient inference but often exhibit weaker reasoning and decision-making performance in socially complex environments. Achieving both strong reasoning ability and efficiency remains an open challenge. To bridge this gap, we propose Group Competitive Learning (GCL), a strategy designed to amplify the capabilities of lightweight VLMs. Our strategy introduces the Group Competitive Objective (GCO) to harmonize global semantics with distributional regularization, alongside Asymmetric Group Optimization (AGO) to explore the upper limits of model performance. Empirical evaluations on social navigation benchmarks demonstrate that GCL significantly elevates VLM performance. Specifically, GCL enables the Qwen2.5-VL-3B learner model and guide Qwen3-VL-4B to achieve an F1 score of 0.968 and 0.914, representing 40\% and 12\% improvement over vanilla supervised fine-tuning (SFT). Notably, under vanilla SFT, the 3B model initially trails the 8B model (F1: 0.692 vs. 0.755). However, through the GCL, the 3B model outperforms (28\%) the 8B baseline model. These results suggest that GCL provides an effective solution for achieving both high accuracy and computational efficiency in real-world deployment.

AI.tldr: Group Competitive Learning (GCL) enhances lightweight Vision Language Models for social robot navigation by improving reasoning capabilities while maintaining computational efficiency, enabling smaller models to outperform larger baselines.
AI.motivation: There's a trade-off between model size and computational efficiency in Vision Language Models for social robot navigation. Large VLMs have strong reasoning but high computational overhead, while lightweight VLMs are efficient but have weaker reasoning in complex social environments. The challenge is achieving both strong reasoning ability and efficiency for real-time robotic deployment.
AI.method: Proposes Group Competitive Learning (GCL) with two components: 1) Group Competitive Objective (GCO) harmonizes global semantics with distributional regularization, and 2) Asymmetric Group Optimization (AGO) explores the upper limits of model performance. The approach amplifies capabilities of lightweight VLMs without increasing model size.
AI.result: GCL significantly elevates VLM performance on social navigation benchmarks. Qwen2.5-VL-3B achieves F1 score of 0.968 (40% improvement over vanilla SFT), and Qwen3-VL-4B achieves 0.914 (12% improvement). Notably, the 3B model with GCL outperforms the 8B baseline model by 28%, demonstrating that smaller models can surpass larger ones with proper training strategy.
AI.conclusion: Group Competitive Learning provides an effective solution for achieving both high accuracy and computational efficiency in real-world deployment of social robot navigation systems, enabling lightweight VLMs to match or exceed the performance of larger models while maintaining inference efficiency.

title: Deactivating Refusal Triggers: Understanding and Mitigating Overrefusal in Safety Alignment
summary: Safety alignment aims to ensure that large language models (LLMs) refuse harmful requests by post-training on harmful queries paired with refusal answers. Although safety alignment is widely adopted in industry, the overrefusal problem where aligned LLMs also reject benign queries after safety alignment post-training, remains insufficiently studied. Such an issue degrades the usability of safety alignment in real-world applications. In this paper, we examine how overrefusal arises under safety alignment, and propose a mitigation strategy inspired by our findings. We define refusal triggers as linguistic cues in the training data that elicit refusal responses, safety alignment encourages LLMs to associate refusal triggers within a training sample with refusal responses, leading aligned LLMs to refuse harmful queries. However, the refusal triggers include not only harmful linguistic cues but also non-harmful cues, therefore causing overrefusal to benign queries. Building on this mechanistic analysis, we propose a method that explicitly considers refusal triggers in the safety alignment fine-tuning. Empirical results demonstrate that our approach achieves a more favorable trade-off between defense against jailbreak attacks and responsiveness to benign queries, outperforming prior methods. Warning: this paper contains harmful and biased sentences.

AI.tldr: Safety alignment in LLMs causes overrefusal to benign queries due to non-harmful refusal triggers in training data; proposed method explicitly addresses refusal triggers to improve trade-off between safety and usability.
AI.motivation: Safety alignment post-training causes LLMs to refuse both harmful and benign queries (overrefusal), degrading usability in real-world applications despite being widely adopted in industry.
AI.method: Mechanistic analysis identifies refusal triggers (linguistic cues in training data) as cause of overrefusal; proposes method that explicitly considers refusal triggers during safety alignment fine-tuning to distinguish harmful from non-harmful cues.
AI.result: Empirical results show the proposed approach achieves better trade-off between defense against jailbreak attacks and responsiveness to benign queries, outperforming prior methods.
AI.conclusion: Overrefusal stems from LLMs associating both harmful and non-harmful refusal triggers with refusal responses; explicitly addressing refusal triggers in safety alignment improves the safety-usability trade-off.

title: CoViLLM: An Adaptive Human-Robot Collaborative Assembly Framework Using Large Language Models for Manufacturing
comment: 7 pages, 7 figures. Accepted to ASME MSEC 2026
summary: With increasing demand for mass customization, traditional manufacturing robots that rely on rule-based operations lack the flexibility to accommodate customized or new product variants. Human-Robot Collaboration (HRC) has demonstrated potential to improve system adaptability by leveraging human versatility and decision-making capabilities. However, existing HRC frame- works typically depend on predefined perception-manipulation pipelines, limiting their ability to autonomously generate task plans for new product assembly. In this work, we propose CoViLLM, an adaptive human-robot collaborative assembly frame- work that supports the assembly of customized and previously unseen products. CoViLLM combines depth-camera-based localization for object position estimation, human operator classification for identifying new components, and an Large Language Model (LLM) for assembly task planning based on natural language instructions. The framework is validated on the NIST Assembly Task Board for known, customized, and new product cases. Experimental results show that the proposed framework enables flexible collaborative assembly by extending HRC beyond predefined product and task settings.

AI.tldr: CoViLLM is an adaptive human-robot collaborative assembly framework that uses LLMs for task planning to enable assembly of customized and previously unseen products, overcoming limitations of traditional rule-based HRC systems.
AI.motivation: Traditional manufacturing robots lack flexibility for mass customization, and existing HRC frameworks are limited by predefined perception-manipulation pipelines that cannot autonomously generate task plans for new product variants.
AI.method: CoViLLM combines depth-camera-based object localization, human operator classification for identifying new components, and Large Language Models for assembly task planning based on natural language instructions.
AI.result: The framework was validated on the NIST Assembly Task Board for known, customized, and new product cases, demonstrating flexible collaborative assembly that extends HRC beyond predefined product and task settings.
AI.conclusion: CoViLLM enables adaptive human-robot collaboration for customized product assembly by integrating LLM-based task planning with perception systems, overcoming limitations of traditional rule-based approaches.

title: Entropy Guided Diversification and Preference Elicitation in Agentic Recommendation Systems
comment: In proceeding to 2026 Association for the Advancement of Artificial Intelligence Spring Symposia
summary: Users on e-commerce platforms can be uncertain about their preferences early in their search. Queries to recommendation systems are frequently ambiguous, incomplete, or weakly specified. Agentic systems are expected to proactively reason, ask clarifying questions, and act on the user's behalf, which makes handling such ambiguity increasingly important. In existing platforms, ambiguity led to excessive interactions and question fatigue or overconfident recommendations prematurely collapsing the search space. We present an Interactive Decision Support System (IDSS) that addresses ambiguous user queries using entropy as a unifying signal. IDSS maintains a dynamically filtered candidate product set and quantifies uncertainty over item attributes using entropy. This uncertainty guides adaptive preference elicitation by selecting follow-up questions that maximize expected information gain. When preferences remain incomplete, IDSS explicitly incorporates residual uncertainty into downstream recommendations through uncertainty-aware ranking and entropy-based diversification, rather than forcing premature resolution. We evaluate IDSS using review-driven simulated users grounded in real user reviews, enabling a controlled study of diverse shopping behaviors. Our evaluation measures both interaction efficiency and recommendation quality. Results show that entropy-guided elicitation reduces unnecessary follow-up questions, while uncertainty-aware ranking and presentation yield more informative, diverse, and transparent recommendation sets under ambiguous intent. These findings demonstrate that entropy-guided reasoning provides an effective foundation for agentic recommendation systems operating under uncertainty.

AI.tldr: IDSS uses entropy to handle ambiguous e-commerce queries by maintaining uncertainty over preferences, adaptively eliciting preferences via information-gain questions, and incorporating residual uncertainty into recommendations through uncertainty-aware ranking and diversification.
AI.motivation: E-commerce users often have ambiguous, incomplete, or weakly specified preferences early in search. Existing systems either ask too many questions (causing fatigue) or make overconfident recommendations that prematurely collapse the search space, highlighting the need for better handling of uncertainty in agentic recommendation systems.
AI.method: IDSS maintains a dynamically filtered candidate product set and quantifies uncertainty over item attributes using entropy. This uncertainty guides adaptive preference elicitation by selecting follow-up questions that maximize expected information gain. When preferences remain incomplete, IDSS explicitly incorporates residual uncertainty into downstream recommendations through uncertainty-aware ranking and entropy-based diversification.
AI.result: Evaluation using review-driven simulated users grounded in real user reviews shows that entropy-guided elicitation reduces unnecessary follow-up questions, while uncertainty-aware ranking and presentation yield more informative, diverse, and transparent recommendation sets under ambiguous intent.
AI.conclusion: Entropy-guided reasoning provides an effective foundation for agentic recommendation systems operating under uncertainty, balancing interaction efficiency with recommendation quality while avoiding premature resolution of ambiguous preferences.

title: NFPO: Stabilized Policy Optimization of Normalizing Flow for Robotic Policy Learning
summary: Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) has experienced significant advancements in recent years and has been widely used in many fields. In DRL-based robotic policy learning, however, current de facto policy parameterization is still multivariate Gaussian (with diagonal covariance matrix), which lacks the ability to model multi-modal distribution. In this work, we explore the adoption of a modern network architecture, i.e. Normalizing Flow (NF) as the policy parameterization for its ability of multi-modal modeling, closed form of log probability and low computation and memory overhead. However, naively training NF in online Reinforcement Learning (RL) usually leads to training instability. We provide a detailed analysis for this phenomenon and successfully address it via simple but effective technique. With extensive experiments in multiple simulation environments, we show our method, NFPO could obtain robust and strong performance in widely used robotic learning tasks and successfully transfer into real-world robots.

AI.tldr: NFPO: Using Normalizing Flows for multi-modal policy parameterization in deep reinforcement learning for robotics, addressing training instability with simple techniques.
AI.motivation: Current DRL for robotics uses multivariate Gaussian policies with diagonal covariance, which cannot model multi-modal distributions needed for complex robotic tasks.
AI.method: Proposes NFPO using Normalizing Flows as policy parameterization for multi-modal modeling, with closed-form log probability and low overhead. Addresses training instability in online RL with simple but effective techniques.
AI.result: Extensive experiments in multiple simulation environments show NFPO obtains robust and strong performance in robotic learning tasks and successfully transfers to real-world robots.
AI.conclusion: Normalizing Flows provide effective multi-modal policy parameterization for DRL in robotics when training instability is properly addressed, enabling successful real-world deployment.

title: Speak or Stay Silent: Context-Aware Turn-Taking in Multi-Party Dialogue
summary: Existing voice AI assistants treat every detected pause as an invitation to speak. This works in dyadic dialogue, but in multi-party settings, where an AI assistant participates alongside multiple speakers, pauses are abundant and ambiguous. An assistant that speaks on every pause becomes disruptive rather than useful. In this work, we formulate context-aware turn-taking: at every detected pause, given the full conversation context, our method decides whether the assistant should speak or stay silent. We introduce a benchmark of over 120K labeled conversations spanning three multi-party corpora. Evaluating eight recent large language models, we find that they consistently fail at context-aware turn-taking under zero-shot prompting. We then propose a supervised fine-tuning approach with reasoning traces, improving balanced accuracy by up to 23 percentage points. Our findings suggest that context-aware turn-taking is not an emergent capability; it must be explicitly trained.

AI.tldr: AI assistants need context-aware turn-taking in multi-party conversations to avoid disruptive interruptions during ambiguous pauses.
AI.motivation: Current voice AI assistants treat every pause as an invitation to speak, which works in dyadic dialogue but becomes disruptive in multi-party settings where pauses are abundant and ambiguous.
AI.method: Formulated context-aware turn-taking problem, created benchmark of 120K labeled conversations from three multi-party corpora, evaluated eight LLMs under zero-shot prompting, then proposed supervised fine-tuning approach with reasoning traces.
AI.result: LLMs consistently fail at context-aware turn-taking under zero-shot prompting; supervised fine-tuning with reasoning traces improved balanced accuracy by up to 23 percentage points.
AI.conclusion: Context-aware turn-taking is not an emergent capability of LLMs and must be explicitly trained through supervised fine-tuning with reasoning traces.

title: SPARK: Skeleton-Parameter Aligned Retargeting on Humanoid Robots with Kinodynamic Trajectory Optimization
summary: Human motion provides rich priors for training general-purpose humanoid control policies, but raw demonstrations are often incompatible with a robot's kinematics and dynamics, limiting their direct use. We present a two-stage pipeline for generating natural and dynamically feasible motion references from task-space human data. First, we convert human motion into a unified robot description format (URDF)-based skeleton representation and calibrate it to the target humanoid's dimensions. By aligning the underlying skeleton structure rather than heuristically modifying task-space targets, this step significantly reduces inverse kinematics error and tuning effort. Second, we refine the retargeted trajectories through progressive kinodynamic trajectory optimization (TO), solved in three stages: kinematic TO, inverse dynamics, and full kinodynamic TO, each warm-started from the previous solution. The final result yields dynamically consistent state trajectories and joint torque profiles, providing high-quality references for learning-based controllers. Together, skeleton calibration and kinodynamic TO enable the generation of natural, physically consistent motion references across diverse humanoid platforms.

AI.tldr: Two-stage pipeline for generating natural, dynamically feasible motion references from human demonstrations for humanoid robots, using skeleton calibration and progressive kinodynamic trajectory optimization.
AI.motivation: Human motion provides rich priors for training humanoid control policies, but raw demonstrations are incompatible with robot kinematics and dynamics, limiting direct use. Need to generate natural and dynamically feasible motion references from task-space human data.
AI.method: Two-stage pipeline: 1) Convert human motion to URDF-based skeleton representation and calibrate to target humanoid dimensions, aligning skeleton structure to reduce IK error. 2) Refine trajectories through progressive kinodynamic trajectory optimization in three stages: kinematic TO, inverse dynamics, and full kinodynamic TO, each warm-started from previous solution.
AI.result: Generates dynamically consistent state trajectories and joint torque profiles, providing high-quality references for learning-based controllers. Enables natural, physically consistent motion references across diverse humanoid platforms.
AI.conclusion: Skeleton calibration and kinodynamic trajectory optimization together enable generation of natural, physically consistent motion references from human demonstrations for various humanoid robots, overcoming incompatibility issues between human and robot kinematics/dynamics.

title: Adversarial Reinforcement Learning for Detecting False Data Injection Attacks in Vehicular Routing
summary: In modern transportation networks, adversaries can manipulate routing algorithms using false data injection attacks, such as simulating heavy traffic with multiple devices running crowdsourced navigation applications, to mislead vehicles toward suboptimal routes and increase congestion. To address these threats, we formulate a strategically zero-sum game between an attacker, who injects such perturbations, and a defender, who detects anomalies based on the observed travel times of network edges. We propose a computational method based on multi-agent reinforcement learning to compute a Nash equilibrium of this game, providing an optimal detection strategy, which ensures that total travel time remains within a worst-case bound, even in the presence of an attack. We present an extensive experimental evaluation that demonstrates the robustness and practical benefits of our approach, providing a powerful framework to improve the resilience of transportation networks against false data injection. In particular, we show that our approach yields approximate equilibrium policies and significantly outperforms baselines for both the attacker and the defender.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a game-theoretic approach using multi-agent reinforcement learning to defend transportation networks against false data injection attacks that manipulate routing algorithms.
AI.motivation: Adversaries can manipulate routing algorithms in modern transportation networks through false data injection attacks, such as simulating heavy traffic using multiple devices running crowdsourced navigation apps, to mislead vehicles toward suboptimal routes and increase congestion.
AI.method: Formulates a strategically zero-sum game between an attacker (injecting perturbations) and a defender (detecting anomalies based on observed travel times). Uses multi-agent reinforcement learning to compute Nash equilibrium, providing optimal detection strategy that ensures total travel time remains within worst-case bounds even under attack.
AI.result: Extensive experimental evaluation demonstrates robustness and practical benefits, showing the approach yields approximate equilibrium policies and significantly outperforms baselines for both attacker and defender.
AI.conclusion: Provides a powerful framework to improve transportation network resilience against false data injection attacks through game-theoretic reinforcement learning approach.

title: MiNI-Q: A Miniature, Wire-Free Quadruped with Unbounded, Independently Actuated Leg Joints
comment: 7 pages, 11 figures. Submitted to the IEEE RAS Conference on Ubiquitous Robots (UR 2026)
summary: Physical joint limits are common in legged robots and can restrict workspace, constrain gait design, and increase the risk of hardware damage. This paper introduces MiNI-Q^2, a miniature, wire-free quadruped robot with independently actuated, mechanically unbounded 2-DOF leg joints. We present the mechanical design, kinematic analysis, and experimental validation of the proposed robot. The leg mechanism enables both oscillatory gaits and rotary locomotion while allowing the robot to fold to a minimum height of 2.5 cm. Experimentally, MiNI-Q achieves speeds up to 0.46 m/s and demonstrates low-clearance crawling, stair climbing, inverted locomotion, jumping, and backflipping. The wire-free architecture extends our previous Q8bot design, improving assembly reliability at miniature scale. All mechanical and electrical design files are released open source to support reproducibility and further research.

AI.tldr: MiNI-Q² is a miniature wire-free quadruped robot with mechanically unbounded 2-DOF leg joints that enables diverse locomotion capabilities including crawling, stair climbing, inverted motion, jumping, and backflipping.
AI.motivation: Physical joint limits in legged robots restrict workspace, constrain gait design, and increase hardware damage risk. The authors aim to overcome these limitations with mechanically unbounded joints.
AI.method: Developed MiNI-Q² with independently actuated, mechanically unbounded 2-DOF leg joints; presented mechanical design, kinematic analysis, and experimental validation; extended wire-free architecture from previous Q8bot design for improved assembly reliability.
AI.result: Robot achieves speeds up to 0.46 m/s, demonstrates low-clearance crawling, stair climbing, inverted locomotion, jumping, and backflipping, and folds to minimum height of 2.5 cm. All design files released open source.
AI.conclusion: MiNI-Q² successfully demonstrates the advantages of mechanically unbounded leg joints for miniature quadruped robots, enabling versatile locomotion capabilities while maintaining compact form factor and wire-free operation.

title: GPT4o-Receipt: A Dataset and Human Study for AI-Generated Document Forensics
summary: Can humans detect AI-generated financial documents better than machines? We present GPT4o-Receipt, a benchmark of 1,235 receipt images pairing GPT-4o-generated receipts with authentic ones from established datasets, evaluated by five state-of-the-art multimodal LLMs and a 30-annotator crowdsourced perceptual study. Our findings reveal a striking paradox: humans are better at seeing AI artifacts, yet worse at detecting AI documents. Human annotators exhibit the largest visual discrimination gap of any evaluator, yet their binary detection F1 falls well below Claude Sonnet 4 and below Gemini 2.5 Flash. This paradox resolves once the mechanism is understood: the dominant forensic signals in AI-generated receipts are arithmetic errors -- invisible to visual inspection but systematically verifiable by LLMs. Humans cannot perceive that a subtotal is incorrect; LLMs verify it in milliseconds. Beyond the human--LLM comparison, our five-model evaluation reveals dramatic performance disparities and calibration differences that render simple accuracy metrics insufficient for detector selection. GPT4o-Receipt, the evaluation framework, and all results are released publicly to support future research in AI document forensics.

AI.tldr: Humans are better at seeing visual AI artifacts but worse at detecting AI-generated financial documents than LLMs due to invisible arithmetic errors that LLMs can systematically verify.
AI.motivation: To understand whether humans or machines are better at detecting AI-generated financial documents, specifically receipts, and to identify the mechanisms behind detection capabilities.
AI.method: Created GPT4o-Receipt benchmark with 1,235 receipt images pairing GPT-4o-generated receipts with authentic ones; evaluated using five state-of-the-art multimodal LLMs and a 30-annotator crowdsourced perceptual study.
AI.result: Humans show the largest visual discrimination gap but have lower binary detection F1 scores than Claude Sonnet 4 and Gemini 2.5 Flash; LLMs outperform humans because they can detect invisible arithmetic errors that humans cannot perceive visually.
AI.conclusion: The paradox resolves when understanding that dominant forensic signals are arithmetic errors invisible to visual inspection but verifiable by LLMs; simple accuracy metrics are insufficient for detector selection due to dramatic performance disparities and calibration differences.

title: RoboClaw: An Agentic Framework for Scalable Long-Horizon Robotic Tasks
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) systems have shown strong potential for language-driven robotic manipulation. However, scaling them to long-horizon tasks remains challenging. Existing pipelines typically separate data collection, policy learning, and deployment, resulting in heavy reliance on manual environment resets and brittle multi-policy execution. We present RoboClaw, an agentic robotics framework that unifies data collection, policy learning, and task execution under a single VLM-driven controller. At the policy level, RoboClaw introduces Entangled Action Pairs (EAP), which couple forward manipulation behaviors with inverse recovery actions to form self-resetting loops for autonomous data collection. This mechanism enables continuous on-policy data acquisition and iterative policy refinement with minimal human intervention. During deployment, the same agent performs high-level reasoning and dynamically orchestrates learned policy primitives to accomplish long-horizon tasks. By maintaining consistent contextual semantics across collection and execution, RoboClaw reduces mismatch between the two phases and improves multi-policy robustness. Experiments in real-world manipulation tasks demonstrate improved stability and scalability compared to conventional open-loop pipelines, while significantly reducing human effort throughout the robot lifecycle, achieving a 25% improvement in success rate over baseline methods on long-horizon tasks and reducing human time investment by 53.7%.

AI.tldr: RoboClaw is a VLA framework that unifies data collection, policy learning, and task execution under a single VLM controller using Entangled Action Pairs for autonomous self-resetting, enabling continuous on-policy learning and robust long-horizon task execution.
AI.motivation: Existing VLA systems for robotic manipulation face challenges in scaling to long-horizon tasks due to separated pipelines for data collection, policy learning, and deployment, which require manual environment resets and suffer from brittle multi-policy execution.
AI.method: RoboClaw introduces Entangled Action Pairs (EAP) that couple forward manipulation behaviors with inverse recovery actions to form self-resetting loops for autonomous data collection. The framework uses a single VLM-driven controller that performs high-level reasoning and dynamically orchestrates learned policy primitives during deployment.
AI.result: Experiments show 25% improvement in success rate over baseline methods on long-horizon tasks and 53.7% reduction in human time investment. The framework demonstrates improved stability and scalability compared to conventional open-loop pipelines.
AI.conclusion: RoboClaw successfully addresses the scalability challenges of VLA systems by unifying data collection, policy learning, and execution under a single controller with self-resetting mechanisms, significantly reducing human effort while improving robustness for long-horizon manipulation tasks.

title: Verified Multi-Agent Orchestration: A Plan-Execute-Verify-Replan Framework for Complex Query Resolution
summary: We present Verified Multi-Agent Orchestration (VMAO), a framework that coordinates specialized LLM-based agents through a verification-driven iterative loop. Given a complex query, our system decomposes it into a directed acyclic graph (DAG) of sub-questions, executes them through domain-specific agents in parallel, verifies result completeness via LLM-based evaluation, and adaptively replans to address gaps. The key contributions are: (1) dependency-aware parallel execution over a DAG of sub-questions with automatic context propagation, (2) verification-driven adaptive replanning that uses an LLM-based verifier as an orchestration-level coordination signal, and (3) configurable stop conditions that balance answer quality against resource usage. On 25 expert-curated market research queries, VMAO improves answer completeness from 3.1 to 4.2 and source quality from 2.6 to 4.1 (1-5 scale) compared to a single-agent baseline, demonstrating that orchestration-level verification is an effective mechanism for multi-agent quality assurance.

AI.tldr: VMAO is a multi-agent LLM framework that uses verification-driven iterative loops to coordinate specialized agents through DAG-based decomposition, parallel execution, and adaptive replanning for complex queries.
AI.motivation: To address the challenge of ensuring high-quality, complete answers for complex queries using LLM-based multi-agent systems, where coordination and quality assurance mechanisms are needed to improve answer completeness and source quality.
AI.method: Decomposes complex queries into DAG of sub-questions, executes them in parallel through domain-specific agents, verifies result completeness via LLM-based evaluation, and adaptively replans to address gaps with configurable stop conditions.
AI.result: On 25 expert-curated market research queries, VMAO improves answer completeness from 3.1 to 4.2 and source quality from 2.6 to 4.1 (1-5 scale) compared to single-agent baseline, demonstrating effective orchestration-level verification.
AI.conclusion: Verification-driven adaptive replanning with LLM-based verifiers serves as an effective coordination mechanism for multi-agent quality assurance, significantly improving answer completeness and source quality for complex queries.

title: Unsupervised LiDAR-Based Multi-UAV Detection and Tracking Under Extreme Sparsity
comment: Presented at the International Conference on Mechatronics and Robotics Engineering (ICMRE2026). To appear in IEEE conference proceedings
summary: Non-repetitive solid-state LiDAR scanning leads to an extremely sparse measurement regime for detecting airborne UAVs: a small quadrotor at 10-25 m typically produces only 1-2 returns per scan, which is far below the point densities assumed by most existing detection approaches and inadequate for robust multi-target data association. We introduce an unsupervised, LiDAR-only pipeline that addresses both detection and tracking without the need for labeled training data. The detector integrates range-adaptive DBSCAN clustering with a three-stage temporal consistency check and is benchmarked on real-world air-to-air flight data under eight different parameter configurations. The best setup attains 0.891 precision, 0.804 recall, and 0.63 m RMSE, and a systematic minPts sweep verifies that most scans contain at most 1-2 target points, directly quantifying the sparsity regime. For multi-target tracking, we compare deterministic Hungarian assignment with joint probabilistic data association (JPDA), each coupled with Interacting Multiple Model filtering, in four simulated scenarios with increasing levels of ambiguity. JPDA cuts identity switches by 64% with negligible impact on MOTA, demonstrating that probabilistic association is advantageous when UAV trajectories approach one another closely. A two-environment evaluation strategy, combining real-world detection with RTK-GPS ground truth and simulation-based tracking with identity-annotated ground truth, overcomes the limitations of GNSS-only evaluation at inter-UAV distances below 2 m.

AI.tldr: Unsupervised LiDAR-only pipeline for detecting and tracking airborne UAVs using sparse point clouds from solid-state LiDAR, with range-adaptive DBSCAN clustering and probabilistic data association for multi-target tracking.
AI.motivation: Solid-state LiDAR scanning produces extremely sparse measurements for airborne UAV detection (1-2 returns per scan), which is inadequate for existing detection approaches and robust multi-target data association, requiring an unsupervised solution without labeled training data.
AI.method: Unsupervised LiDAR-only pipeline with range-adaptive DBSCAN clustering and three-stage temporal consistency check for detection. For tracking, compares deterministic Hungarian assignment with joint probabilistic data association (JPDA), both coupled with Interacting Multiple Model filtering. Uses two-environment evaluation combining real-world detection with RTK-GPS ground truth and simulation-based tracking.
AI.result: Best detection setup achieves 0.891 precision, 0.804 recall, and 0.63 m RMSE. JPDA reduces identity switches by 64% with negligible impact on MOTA compared to Hungarian assignment, demonstrating advantage in ambiguous scenarios with closely approaching UAV trajectories.
AI.conclusion: The proposed unsupervised pipeline effectively addresses sparse LiDAR measurements for UAV detection and tracking, with probabilistic data association significantly improving identity maintenance in ambiguous multi-target scenarios, overcoming limitations of GNSS-only evaluation at close inter-UAV distances.

title: Examining Users' Behavioural Intention to Use OpenClaw Through the Cognition--Affect--Conation Framework
summary: This study examines users' behavioural intention to use OpenClaw through the Cognition--Affect--Conation (CAC) framework. The research investigates how cognitive perceptions of the system influence affective responses and subsequently shape behavioural intention. Enabling factors include perceived personalisation, perceived intelligence, and relative advantage, while inhibiting factors include privacy concern, algorithmic opacity, and perceived risk. Survey data from 436 OpenClaw users were analysed using structural equation modelling. The results show that positive perceptions strengthen users' attitudes toward OpenClaw, which increase behavioural intention, whereas negative perceptions increase distrust and reduce intention to use the system. The study provides insights into the psychological mechanisms influencing the adoption of autonomous AI agents.

AI.tldr: Users' intention to use OpenClaw AI agent is influenced by cognitive perceptions affecting emotions and behavior, with enabling factors (personalization, intelligence, advantage) increasing adoption and inhibiting factors (privacy, opacity, risk) decreasing it.
AI.motivation: To understand the psychological mechanisms driving adoption of autonomous AI agents like OpenClaw, specifically examining how cognitive perceptions influence affective responses and behavioral intentions through the Cognition-Affect-Conation framework.
AI.method: Survey of 436 OpenClaw users analyzed using structural equation modeling within the CAC framework, examining enabling factors (perceived personalization, intelligence, relative advantage) and inhibiting factors (privacy concern, algorithmic opacity, perceived risk).
AI.result: Positive cognitive perceptions strengthen attitudes toward OpenClaw and increase behavioral intention, while negative perceptions increase distrust and reduce intention to use. The CAC framework effectively explains adoption mechanisms.
AI.conclusion: The study provides insights into psychological mechanisms influencing autonomous AI agent adoption, showing that cognitive perceptions drive affective responses which shape behavioral intentions, with both enabling and inhibiting factors playing crucial roles.

title: Diversity You Can Actually Measure: A Fast, Model-Free Diversity Metric for Robotics Datasets
summary: Robotics datasets for imitation learning typically consist of long-horizon trajectories of different lengths over states, actions, and high-dimensional observations (e.g., RGB video), making it non-trivial to quantify diversity in a way that respects the underlying trajectory structure and geometry. We extend Shannon and von Neumann entropy to this setting by defining signature transform-based entropy on the Gram matrix of a signature kernel over demonstrations, yielding entropy and diversity metrics that operate directly on the demonstration dataset. Building on these metrics, we study how dataset diversity affects generalization performance in robot imitation learning and propose a simple, model-free way to curate diverse demonstrations. We introduce FAKTUAL (FAst trajectory Kernel enTropy cUration for imitation Learning), a data curation algorithm that selects a subset of demonstrations maximizing entropy given a subset-size budget. FAKTUAL is fully model-free, requires no access to the imitation policy or rollouts, and adds negligible overhead relative to policy training. We evaluate our approach on image and state-based RoboMimic and MetaWorld benchmarks, as well as four real-world manipulation tasks. Across tasks and architectures, diversity-aware curation with FAKTUAL consistently improves downstream success rates over random selection, while being substantially more computationally efficient compared to recent robot data curation methods. Our results suggest that the entropy of demonstration datasets is a practical tool for understanding and improving dataset diversity in robot imitation learning.

AI.tldr: FAKTUAL introduces a model-free data curation method for robot imitation learning that uses signature kernel-based entropy to select diverse demonstrations, improving downstream success rates without policy access or training overhead.
AI.motivation: Existing robotics datasets for imitation learning contain trajectories of varying lengths with high-dimensional observations, making it difficult to quantify diversity while respecting trajectory structure and geometry. Current methods lack principled ways to measure and leverage dataset diversity for improved imitation learning performance.
AI.method: Extends Shannon and von Neumann entropy to trajectory data using signature transform-based entropy on Gram matrices of signature kernels over demonstrations. Introduces FAKTUAL (FAst trajectory Kernel enTropy cUration for imitation Learning), a model-free algorithm that selects demonstration subsets maximizing entropy given a budget, requiring no policy access or rollouts.
AI.result: FAKTUAL consistently improves downstream success rates over random selection across image/state-based RoboMimic and MetaWorld benchmarks and four real-world manipulation tasks. It's substantially more computationally efficient than recent robot data curation methods while adding negligible overhead relative to policy training.
AI.conclusion: Signature kernel-based entropy provides a practical tool for understanding and improving dataset diversity in robot imitation learning. FAKTUAL demonstrates that diversity-aware curation with model-free entropy maximization can significantly enhance imitation learning performance across diverse tasks and architectures.

title: Multi-Agent Collaboration for Automated Design Exploration on High Performance Computing Systems
summary: Today's scientific challenges, from climate modeling to Inertial Confinement Fusion design to novel material design, require exploring huge design spaces. In order to enable high-impact scientific discovery, we need to scale up our ability to test hypotheses, generate results, and learn from them rapidly. We present MADA (Multi-Agent Design Assistant), a Large Language Model (LLM) powered multi-agent framework that coordinates specialized agents for complex design workflows. A Job Management Agent (JMA) launches and manages ensemble simulations on HPC systems, a Geometry Agent (GA) generates meshes, and an Inverse Design Agent (IDA) proposes new designs informed by simulation outcomes. While general purpose, we focus development and validation on Richtmyer--Meshkov Instability (RMI) suppression, a critical challenge in Inertial Confinement Fusion. We evaluate on two complementary settings: running a hydrodynamics simulations on HPC systems, and using a pre-trained machine learning surrogate for rapid design exploration. Our results demonstrate that the MADA system successfully executes iterative design refinement, automatically improving designs toward optimal RMI suppression with minimal manual intervention. Our framework reduces cumbersome manual workflow setup, and enables automated design exploration at scale. More broadly, it demonstrates a reusable pattern for coupling reasoning, simulation, specialized tools, and coordinated workflows to accelerate scientific discovery.

AI.tldr: MADA is an LLM-powered multi-agent framework that automates complex scientific design workflows by coordinating specialized agents for simulation management, geometry generation, and inverse design, validated on Richtmyer-Meshkov Instability suppression for fusion applications.
AI.motivation: Scientific challenges like climate modeling, fusion design, and material discovery require exploring vast design spaces, necessitating scalable systems to rapidly test hypotheses, generate results, and learn from them to accelerate high-impact scientific discovery.
AI.method: MADA uses LLM-powered multi-agent coordination with specialized agents: Job Management Agent (JMA) for HPC ensemble simulation management, Geometry Agent (GA) for mesh generation, and Inverse Design Agent (IDA) for design proposals informed by simulation outcomes. Validated on Richtmyer-Meshkov Instability suppression using both HPC hydrodynamics simulations and ML surrogates.
AI.result: The system successfully executes iterative design refinement, automatically improving designs toward optimal RMI suppression with minimal manual intervention. It reduces cumbersome workflow setup and enables automated design exploration at scale.
AI.conclusion: MADA demonstrates a reusable pattern for coupling reasoning, simulation, specialized tools, and coordinated workflows to accelerate scientific discovery, showing promise for automating complex design processes across scientific domains.

title: Learn Structure, Adapt on the Fly: Multi-Scale Residual Learning and Online Adaptation for Aerial Manipulators
summary: Autonomous Aerial Manipulators (AAMs) are inherently coupled, nonlinear systems that exhibit nonstationary and multiscale residual dynamics, particularly during manipulator reconfiguration and abrupt payload variations. Conventional analytical dynamic models rely on fixed parametric structures, while static data-driven model assume stationary dynamics and degrade under configuration changes and payload variations. Moreover, existing learning architectures do not explicitly factorize cross-variable coupling and multi-scale temporal effects, conflating instantaneous inertial dynamics with long-horizon regime evolution. We propose a predictive-adaptive framework for real-time residual modeling and compensation in AAMs. The core of this framework is the Factorized Dynamics Transformer (FDT), which treats physical variables as independent tokens. This design enables explicit cross-variable attention while structurally separating short-horizon inertial dependencies from long-horizon aerodynamic effects. To address deployment-time distribution shifts, a Latent Residual Adapter (LRA) performs rapid linear adaptation in the latent space via Recursive Least Squares, preserving the offline nonlinear representation without prohibitive computational overhead. The adapted residual forecast is directly integrated into a residual-compensated adaptive controller. Real-world experiments on an aerial manipulator subjected to unseen payloads demonstrate higher prediction fidelity, accelerated disturbance attenuation, and superior closed-loop tracking precision compared to state-of-the-art learning baselines, all while maintaining strict real-time feasibility.

AI.tldr: FDT+LRA framework for real-time residual modeling in aerial manipulators, using factorized attention for cross-variable coupling and multi-scale dynamics, with latent adaptation for deployment-time distribution shifts.
AI.motivation: AAMs have complex nonlinear dynamics with nonstationary residuals during manipulator reconfiguration and payload changes. Conventional analytical models have fixed structures, while static data-driven models assume stationarity and degrade under configuration changes. Existing learning methods don't properly factorize cross-variable coupling and multi-scale temporal effects.
AI.method: Proposes Factorized Dynamics Transformer (FDT) that treats physical variables as independent tokens, enabling explicit cross-variable attention while separating short-horizon inertial dependencies from long-horizon aerodynamic effects. Uses Latent Residual Adapter (LRA) for rapid linear adaptation via Recursive Least Squares in latent space to handle deployment-time distribution shifts without computational overhead.
AI.result: Real-world experiments on aerial manipulator with unseen payloads show higher prediction fidelity, accelerated disturbance attenuation, and superior closed-loop tracking precision compared to state-of-the-art learning baselines, while maintaining real-time feasibility.
AI.conclusion: The FDT+LRA framework effectively addresses the challenges of residual modeling in AAMs by factorizing cross-variable coupling and multi-scale dynamics, with latent adaptation enabling robust performance under distribution shifts, demonstrating practical real-time applicability.

title: Expert Threshold Routing for Autoregressive Language Modeling with Dynamic Computation Allocation and Load Balancing
summary: Token-choice Mixture-of-Experts (TC-MoE) routes each token to a fixed number of experts, limiting dynamic computation allocation and requiring auxiliary losses to maintain load balance. We propose Expert Threshold (ET) routing, where each expert maintains an exponential moving average (EMA) threshold estimated from the global token distribution. At both training and inference, each token is independently routed to an expert if its score exceeds the expert's threshold, enabling dynamic computation allocation while achieving load balance without auxiliary losses. This fully causal mechanism eliminates dependence on other tokens in the batch, making it well-suited for autoregressive language modeling. In pretraining experiments scaling to 2.4B parameters on FineWeb-Edu, ET achieves 0.067 lower cross-entropy loss than TC-MoE, equivalent to reaching the same performance with 1.6$\times$ fewer tokens.

AI.tldr: ET routing uses expert-specific thresholds estimated from token distributions to enable dynamic computation allocation and load balance without auxiliary losses, outperforming TC-MoE in language modeling.
AI.motivation: TC-MoE has limitations: fixed token routing restricts dynamic computation allocation and requires auxiliary losses for load balance. The authors seek a more flexible, fully causal routing mechanism suitable for autoregressive language modeling.
AI.method: Expert Threshold (ET) routing: each expert maintains an EMA threshold estimated from global token distribution. Tokens are independently routed to experts if their scores exceed expert thresholds, enabling dynamic allocation without batch dependencies.
AI.result: In 2.4B parameter pretraining on FineWeb-Edu, ET achieves 0.067 lower cross-entropy loss than TC-MoE, equivalent to reaching same performance with 1.6× fewer tokens.
AI.conclusion: ET routing provides superior performance over TC-MoE by enabling dynamic computation allocation while maintaining load balance without auxiliary losses, making it well-suited for autoregressive language modeling.

title: Chunk-Boundary Artifact in Action-Chunked Generative Policies: A Noise-Sensitive Failure Mechanism
summary: Action chunking has become a central design choice for generative visuomotor policies, yet the execution discontinuities that arise at chunk boundaries remain poorly understood. In a frozen pretrained action-chunked policy, we identify chunk-boundary artifact as a noise-sensitive failure mechanism. First, artifact is strongly associated with task failure (p < 1e-4, permutation test) and emerges during the rollout rather than only as a post-hoc symptom. Second, under a fixed observation context, changing only latent noise systematically modulates artifact magnitude. Third, by identifying artifact-related directions in noise space and applying trajectory-level steering, we reliably alter artifact magnitude across all evaluated tasks. In hard-task settings with remaining outcome headroom, the success/failure distribution shifts accordingly; on near-ceiling tasks, positive gains are compressed by policy saturation, while the negative causal effect remains visible. Overall, we recast boundary discontinuity from an unavoidable execution nuisance into an analyzable, noise-dominated, and intervenable failure mechanism.

AI.tldr: Action chunking in visuomotor policies creates execution discontinuities at boundaries that are noise-sensitive failure mechanisms, not just unavoidable nuisances.
AI.motivation: To understand and address the execution discontinuities that arise at chunk boundaries in action-chunked generative visuomotor policies, which are currently poorly understood but central to policy design.
AI.method: Analyzed frozen pretrained action-chunked policies to identify chunk-boundary artifacts as noise-sensitive failure mechanisms. Used statistical tests (p < 1e-4, permutation test), systematic noise modulation, identification of artifact-related directions in noise space, and trajectory-level steering to manipulate artifact magnitude.
AI.result: Chunk-boundary artifacts are strongly associated with task failure, emerge during rollout (not just post-hoc), are systematically modulated by latent noise, and can be reliably altered via noise-space steering. In hard tasks, success/failure distributions shift accordingly; in near-ceiling tasks, positive gains are compressed by policy saturation while negative causal effects remain visible.
AI.conclusion: Boundary discontinuity can be recast from an unavoidable execution nuisance into an analyzable, noise-dominated, and intervenable failure mechanism, enabling systematic analysis and intervention in action-chunked policies.

title: AI Knows What's Wrong But Cannot Fix It: Helicoid Dynamics in Frontier LLMs Under High-Stakes Decisions
summary:
Large language models perform reliably when their outputs can be checked: solving equations, writing code, retrieving facts. They perform differently when checking is impossible, as when a clinician chooses an irreversible treatment on incomplete data, or an investor commits capital under fundamental uncertainty.
  Helicoid dynamics is the name given to a specific failure regime in that second domain: a system engages competently, drifts into error, accurately names what went wrong, then reproduces the same pattern at a higher level of sophistication, recognizing it is looping and continuing nonetheless. This prospective case series documents that regime across seven leading systems (Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, Grok, DeepSeek, Perplexity, Llama families), tested across clinical diagnosis, investment evaluation, and high-consequence interview scenarios. Despite explicit protocols designed to sustain rigorous partnership, all exhibited the pattern. When confronted with it, they attributed its persistence to structural factors in their training, beyond what conversation can reach.
